title: Kashmir
hook: before the valley there was a lake, and in the lake a demon who could not be caught while he stayed in the water

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of Maharashtra's Varkari road: a bow at Vitthal's feet, or to his spire, and then home. What did you pause to mark as finished? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-eight.

Before there was a valley, the old book says, there was a lake. Mountains all around, and water filling the space between them, still and deep. And in that water lived a demon. As long as he stayed in the lake, nobody could touch him, and he came out to raid the lands nearby and slipped back under the surface. The gods couldn't reach him. So how do you defeat someone who hides in the water? You take away the water. This week, Kashmir, and the story it tells about how it began.
screen: `A LAKE BETWEEN MOUNTAINS.` → `A DEMON HIDING IN THE WATER.` → `TAKE AWAY THE WATER.`

segments.voice: The book is the Nilamata Purana, a Sanskrit text of Kashmir, and it tells the valley's beginning like this, here in paraphrase. The lake was called Satisar, the lake of Sati, the goddess. The demon in it was Jalodbhava. He couldn't be killed in his element, so the sage Kashyapa went to the gods and asked for help. Vishnu, Shiva and Brahma came. The mountain wall was opened, the water drained away, and the demon, left on dry ground, was struck down. What was left behind was a green valley, and people came to live in it. Tradition links Kashmir's name with Kashyapa, the sage who asked. Now, what kind of story is this? It's a story about a place, and it treats the land itself as sacred. The valley isn't just where things happen. Its floor was once the goddess's lake. Its waters, the rivers and springs that remained, are holy. Hold onto that, because this week we'll keep meeting holy water and holy places in Kashmir. And look at the shape of the victory. The gods don't fight the demon in the water. They change the ground under him. A danger that hides can't stay hidden when what covers it is drained away. Some readers hear in that an inner meaning too: what lurks under the surface of a mind loses its power once it's brought into the open. And Kashmir became known, in time, as a home of poets and thinkers, some of whom you've met already this year in the Shiva Sutras and in Lal Ded. This week, more of them, starting from the lake.
screen: `THE LAKE OF SATI` · `JALODBHAVA IN THE WATER` · `KASHYAPA ASKS, THE LAKE DRAINS` · `A HOLY VALLEY`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow. Picture a lake between mountains, its surface flat and calm. As you breathe out, let the water level drop a little, and then a little more. Whatever has been sitting under the surface of your mind today, a worry, a grudge, a plan, notice it as the water goes down. You don't have to fight it. Just see it in the open. If you pray, you can offer it up in your own way. The bell holds the time.
Kashmir. The valley that, the Nilamata Purana says, was once the lake of Sati, drained when the sage Kashyapa asked the gods for help. Today's word.
Your line: Kashmir. Today, name out loud, to yourself, one thing that's been hiding under the surface. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Kashmiri Hindus tell the story of Satisar, the lake drained so the demon Jalodbhava could be defeated, as the beginning of the valley, and honor its springs and rivers as sacred.

original.note: Kashyapa in Sanskrit, written in Devanagari: the sage tradition links with Kashmir's name.

trapdoor: what you thought: Kashmir is just a place name on a map.

sources.ref: Nilamata Purana: Satisar, Jalodbhava, Kashyapa and the draining of the lake

notes: Nilamata Purana account: confirm which gods take part (Vishnu, Shiva, Brahma), who opens the mountain (some tellings give Ananta or Vishnu's plough/Balarama), and who kills Jalodbhava (Vishnu). Kalhana's Rajatarangini retells it too.
'Jalodbhava, whose name means born of water': a name gloss; confirm (jala + udbhava).
'Tradition links Kashmir's name with Kashyapa': kept as tradition; this is a popular, not scholarly, etymology.
'Kashmir became known as a home of poets and thinkers' is general framing; no claim of rank made.
